answer: Human evidence on microplastic health effects remains limited and largely observational, with studies mainly reporting associations with biological markers rather than confirmed clinical outcomes [2]. Microplastics may induce inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and cellular damage, potentially contributing to various diseases [2]. Some studies have reported possible associations between microplastics in the body and gastrointestinal complications, inflammatory conditions, hormonal imbalances, and reproductive dysfunction [2]. Direct evidence linking these mechanisms to adverse health outcomes in humans remains limited [2]. Recent investigations have documented microplastics in multiple human biological matrices, including excretory products, respiratory secretions, systemic circulation, vascular tissues, major organs, and placental tissue, indicating their ability to translocate within the human body [3].
